In the 2AFC test, pairs and triplets were presented and participants were instructed to choose the one out of the two possibilities that is more familiar to what they previously saw during the training phase. The 36 trials in the 2AFC test varied in difficulty. In the production test, incomplete triplets were presented and participants were instructed to complete them with one of three items. The production test consisted of 12 trials which varied in the location and/or identity of the missing item within the sequence.

In the segmentation task, SL can be assessed with online and offline measures. Online measure refers to the performance in the training phase; SL was assessed by comparing RTs and accuracy scores between sequence, random and recovery blocks. Just as in the SRT task, learning is reflected in faster and more accurate responses as the sequence blocks progress, a performance disruption in the random block and a recovery of performance when the sequence reappears in the last block. Offline measures refer to the 2AFC and production tests, where above-chance selection and completion of the trained triplets is interpreted as evidence of successful SL.

2.2.4. Temporal Visual Statistical Learning (TVSL) task

In the TVSL task (Siegelman, Bogaerts, & Frost, 2017), a continuous stream of 16 nonfigurative visual shapes was presented sequentially at the center of the screen (Fig. 1D). Prior to familiarization, the shapes were randomly organized for each participant into eight triplets.

Four triplets consisted of four shapes with transitional probabilities of 0.33 between adjacent elements, whereas the remaining four triplets consisted of three unique shapes each, with transitional probabilities of 1 between adjacent elements. During the 10-min familiarization phase, the eight triplets were presented repeatedly in pseudorandom order, with each triplet occurring 24 times and the constraint that the same triplet could not occur consecutively. Each shape was presented for 800 ms, followed by a 200-ms interstimulus interval. Participants were instructed to attend to the visual stream because they would be tested on it subsequently.

Following familiarization, participants completed a 42-item test comprising patternrecognition and pattern-completion trials. In the pattern-recognition trials, participants selected the more familiar pattern from a set of alternatives, including previously presented triplets and foils that had not occurred during familiarization. In the pattern-completion trials, participants selected the shape that correctly completed a partially presented pattern. Note that these measures are conceptually equivalent to the 2AFC and production measures, respectively, used in the other SL tasks. SL was quantified as the proportion of trials on which participants correctly selected the embedded triplets and above-chance selection of the trained triplets is interpreted as evidence of successful SL.

2.2.5. Spatial visual statistical learning (SVSL) task

In the spatial visual SL task (Fiser & Aslin, 2001), participants viewed a sequence of visual scenes containing six unfamiliar, non-figurative shapes arranged in pairs within a 5 × 5 grid during familiarization (Fig. 1E). A total of 212 unique scenes were presented twice, each scene was presented for 2000 ms. Three shape pairs were presented in each scene, with some pairs occurring more frequently than others. Critically, certain pairs of shapes were always presented together in the same spatial arrangement, whereas other pairs occurred together only on half of the occasions when one of their constituent shapes appeared. The overall frequency of occurrence of these pairs was matched, such that distinguishing between them required learning the predictability of one shape from the other rather than simply their frequency of cooccurrence. Participants were instructed to attend to the sequence of scenes but were not informed about the underlying regularities.

Following familiarization, participants completed a 2AFC test with eight trials. On each trial, they viewed two displays: one containing spatial configurations consistent with the statistical structure encountered during familiarization and another containing novel or less probable configurations. Participants were asked to indicate which display appeared more familiar. Above-chance selection of the familiar configurations was interpreted as evidence that participants had implicitly learned the spatial statistical regularities embedded in the scenes.

2.2.6. Contextual cueing task

In the contextual cueing task (Chun & Jiang, 1998b; Jiang & Sisk, 2019), participants searched for a target stimulus embedded among distractors and were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible to a defining feature of the target, namely, the orientation of a rotated letter "T" among 11 rotated "L" distractors (Fig. 1F). Each trial began with the 500ms-long presentation of a fixation point, followed by the search display. The search display remained visible until the participant responded, allowing RT to be measured from display onset to the response. Participants indicated whether the target T was rotated to the left or right.

If participants responded incorrectly, a 2000 ms pause was inserted to reduce the negative impact of an incorrect response on subsequent trials. The next trial started following a 500-ms intertrial interval.

Unknown to the participants, some search configurations were repeated across the experiment, such that the spatial arrangement of the distractors consistently predicted the target location. Other configurations were newly generated on each trial and appeared only once during the task. The former ones are referred to as repeated configurations and the latter as novel configurations. The experimental session consisted of 30 blocks of 24 trials each, resulting in 720 experimental trials. Each block contained 12 repeated and 12 novel configurations, with their order randomized within the block. Across the experiment, the same set of repeated configurations was presented repeatedly, whereas novel configurations were generated such that each appeared only once.

SL was assessed by comparing RTs between repeated and novel configurations. Faster responses to repeated than to novel configurations indicate that participants learned the spatial regularities embedded in the repeated displays and subsequently used the learned context to facilitate target localization. Thus, a larger RT advantage for repeated relative to novel configurations was interpreted as evidence of SL.

2.2.7. Weather Prediction Task (WPT)

In the WPT (Knowlton et al., 1994; Lukács & Kemény, 2015), participants were presented with a combination of one to three cue cards displaying different geometric patterns (Fig. 1G). Their task was to predict one of two possible outcomes ("sun" or "rain") by pressing the corresponding response key. Following each response, feedback indicating the correct outcome was provided.

Unknown to the participants, the cue cards and their combinations were probabilistically associated with the two possible outcomes. Thus, no individual cue or cue combination provided perfectly reliable information about the correct response. Successful performance therefore required participants to gradually learn these cue-outcome associations from trial-by-trial feedback. The task consisted of 200 trials divided into four blocks of 50 trials. Learning was reflected in progressively improved prediction accuracy across the task. In the TVSL task, a continuous stream of non-figurative symbols was presented sequentially at the center of the screen. During the stimulus presentation, participants were instructed to pay attention but they did not need to press any buttons. (E) In the SVSL task, complex visual scenes of abstract shapes arranged within a spatial grid were presented to the participants. They were instructed to pay attention but were not required to make any responses. (F) In the CC task, participants searched for a rotated letter T embedded among rotated L distractors and responded as quickly and accurately as possible to the target's orientation. (G) In the weather prediction task (WPT), participants predicted whether the outcome would be "sun" or "rain" based on combinations of one to three cue cards displaying geometric patterns. Each cue card was probabilistically associated with one of the two outcomes.

2.3. Procedure

Participants completed the tasks in two 2.5-hour-long sessions. In conjunction with the SL tasks, executive functions were also measured to investigate the interplay between the two cognitive functions. The present study focuses solely on SL and its subprocesses, hence, executive functions tasks are not analyzed here and will be reported in a separate paper. To minimize interference between the tasks, we created two fixed sessions, this way, more similar SL tasks were never presented in the same session. In more detail, the ASRT and SRT tasks, as well as the TVSL and SVSL tasks, were always administered in separate sessions to reduce potential carryover between closely related task pairs (the TVSL and SVSL used the same stimuli, whereas the ASRT and SRT shared similar perceptual and response requirements). The order of the two sessions were counterbalanced between participants. To minimize fatigue effect, the order of the tasks within one session were pseudorandom: ten orders were created and randomized across participants.

2.4. Statistical analyses

>Statistical analyses

2.4.1. Quantifying learning in each task

First, to ensure that participants exhibited successful SL in all tasks at the group level, we examined learning in each task. Then, as we aimed to identify the latent structure underlying the SL measures, we created learning indices for the online measures to use in an EFA. For the ASRT (Howard & Howard, 1997), we computed the mean accuracy and median RTs for highand low-probability triplets separately for every five blocks (that is, for Blocks 1-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20 and 21-25). Then, for accuracy, we subtracted scores for low-probability triplets from high-probability ones, while for RTs, we subtracted scores for high-probability triplets from low-probability ones; this way, a higher learning index meant higher learning for both measures. The learning indices calculated for each block bins were then averaged over the whole task.

For the SRT task, out of the 12 blocks, Block 11 was random and the remaining blocks contained the sequence. Hence, to quantify the disruption of performance in the random block, we first computed median RTs for Blocks 10-12, then compared performance in the random block (Block 11) to the average of the surrounding sequence blocks (Block 10 and 12) (Nissen & Bullemer, 1987). Again, a higher learning index meant higher learning. For the SRT task, conventionally, RT is used as the primary learning measure as accuracy is often near the ceiling and therefore less informative about individual differences in learning. Thus, we included only the RT index in the analyses.

For the Segmentation task (Lukács et al., 2021), out of the 5 blocks, Block 4 was random and the remaining blocks contained the sequence. Similarly to the SRT task, we compared performance in the random block (Block 4) to the average of the neighboring blocks (Block 3 and 5). Higher scores indicated better learning. For the offline measures, accuracy indices for the 2AFC and production tests were used separately in the analyses.

For the TVSL task, accuracy indices for the pattern-recognition and pattern-completion tests were used (Siegelman, Bogaerts, & Frost, 2017). For the spatial visual SL task, an accuracy index for the 2AFC test was used (called pair test in Fiser & Aslin, 2001). For the Contextual Cueing task, in each block, we subtracted RTs for repeated trials from RTs for novel trials, then averaged them over the task. Similarly to the SRT task, we only relied on RT measures as accuracy was near the ceiling, thus, less informative about individual differences in learning (Jiang & Sisk, 2019). For the WPT, accuracy scores were averaged over the four blocks (Lukács & Kemény, 2015).

2.4.2. Reliability and correlational analyses

As the present study investigates individual differences in SL, we examined the reliability of the tasks using internal consistency metrics. Following the procedure presented in Farkas et al. (2023), for each task, we created two splits of trials, ensuring that the proportion of different trial types was matched across splits, when applicable (i.e., high vs. low-probability trials in the ASRT task or novel vs. repeated trials in the CC task). We then created the relevant learning score for each participant, separately for the two splits. Finally, we calculated the simple split-half correlation as well as Cronbach's alpha following Green et al. (2016), with Feldt et al.'s (1987) confidence intervals. General guidelines place acceptable reliability for research purposes in the .65 to .90 range, high enough for the measure to be coherent but not so high as to be redundant (Brysbaert, 2024; DeVellis, 2017; Streiner, 2003). Recent consensus work in the SL field has argued against applying a single strict criterion, given that the study of individual differences in SL is still emerging, recommending instead that reliability be reported for every measure and that its consequences for statistical power be considered explicitly (Bogaerts et al., 2025).

After computing the learning indices and reliability for each task, we ran a correlational analysis to explore their relation to each other. Because imperfect reliability attenuates observed correlations (Krajcsi, 2026; Revelle & Condon, 2019), we report both uncorrected and reliability-corrected correlations, and also apply the Bonferroni correction to control for multiple comparisons. Bayesian correlation analyses were also conducted using the BayesFactor package in R, with a default Cauchy prior (scale = 1/3) on the correlation coefficient.

2.4.3. Exploratory factor analysis

We aimed to identify the latent structure underlying the sets of SL measures in a datadriven manner. Therefore, we examined the factor structure of the SL measures using maximum likelihood (ML) EFA with oblimin rotation, as implemented in the psych package in R with default settings (Revelle & Revelle, 2015). To evaluate the suitability of the data for factor analysis, we applied three complementary procedures (Dziuban & Shirkey, 1974). First, individual measures of sampling adequacy (MSA) were inspected to evaluate whether each variable met the recommended threshold of .50. Second, we calculated the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy (Kaiser, 1970). Higher overall KMO values indicate greater suitability for factor analysis; while Kaiser (Kaiser, 1970) originally recommended a cut-off of .60, lower thresholds of .50 have also been proposed (Dziuban & Shirkey, 1974). Third, we conducted Bartlett's test of sphericity, which evaluates the null hypothesis that the sample correlation matrix originates from a multivariate normal population in which the variables are uncorrelated (Bartlett, 1950). Rejection of this hypothesis indicates that the data are appropriate for factor analysis.

The number of factors to retain was determined using Horn's parallel analysis (Horn, 1965). This method compares the eigenvalues obtained from the observed data with those derived from randomly generated datasets of identical size. Factors were retained when their observed eigenvalues exceeded those obtained from the random data. To apply a more conservative criterion, we compared the observed eigenvalues to the 95th percentile, rather than the mean, of the simulated eigenvalue distributions.

Moreover, using ML EFA allowed us to calculate multiple fit indices of the applied factor analytic models. We chose to focus on the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation and .08 an acceptable fit and values greater than .10 a poor fit. Similarly, SRMR values below .05 constitute a good fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999).

3. Results

>Results

3.1. Learning on the SL tasks

First, we examined whether participants acquired the statistical regularities embedded in each SL task. Results indicated significant learning in nearly all tasks, with learning in the SVSL task reaching only trend-level significance. Overall, these findings provide support for successful acquisition of the SL regularities across the employed paradigms (Fig. 2). Detailed analyses for each task are reported in the Supplementary Information (Section 1.1.). panels E, F, and K indicate chance-level reference values for the respective tasks. For the TVSL task (panels H and I), chance level was determined jointly for the 2AFC and production measures and is therefore not indicated in the figure. For details, see Supplementary Information.

3.2. Reliability of the SL measures

To establish the reliability of the employed tasks, split-half reliability analyses were conducted for all SL variables (for details, see Statistical analyses section). Reliability estimates varied across measures (Cronbach's α = .50 to .96). Most indices fell within or above the conventionally acceptable range and were broadly comparable to previously published estimates for the same paradigms, including split-half values around .60 for the ASRT and SRT and around .75 to .85 for offline measures (Bogaerts et al., 2025; Farkas et al., 2023; Siegelman & Frost, 2015); the TVSL pattern-completion score was an exception, showing insufficient reliability (α = .50). Reliability estimates for each task are presented in Figure 3.

3.3. Associations among SL measures

To examine the relationships among the SL measures, we calculated both the uncorrected and reliability-corrected correlations between all variables. To control for the multiple comparisons, Bonferroni correction was used. The resulting correlation matrix is presented in Figure 4.

Overall, correlations were predominantly observed between measures originating from the same task, with moderate to strong positive associations among task-specific indices.

Cross-task associations were relatively sparse and generally weak. Specifically, the offline measures of the Segmentation and TVSL tasks showed a weak positive correlation, while performance on the TVSL and SVSL tasks was moderately positively correlated. Additionally, one offline measure of the Segmentation task exhibited a weak positive correlation with WPT performance. Taken together, the pattern of correlations suggests limited convergence across different SL paradigms.

Bayesian analyses supported this pattern: although several small cross-paradigm associations received evidence in favor of an association, most remaining cross-paradigm comparisons provided moderate evidence in favor of the null rather than merely inconclusive evidence (Section 1.2. and Fig. S7 in the Supplementary Information).

3.4. Exploratory factor analysis of SL measures

Prior to conducting the EFA, we assessed the factorability of the data. Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant, χ²(66) = 434.49, p < .001, indicating that the correlation matrix differed from an identity matrix, making it suitable for EFA. The overall KMO measure of sampling adequacy was .59, suggesting marginal but acceptable suitability for factor analysis (Dziuban & Shirkey, 1974). Most variables exhibited individual MSA above the recommended threshold of .50; however, four variables fell slightly below this criterion (lowest MSA = .42).

Although these findings suggest that some measures shared limited common variance with the remaining variables, the overall pattern of results supported proceeding with factor analysis.

Hence, to examine the latent structure of the SL measures, an ML EFA employing oblimin rotation was performed.

To determine the number of factors to extract, we conducted a parallel analysis.

Comparison of the observed eigenvalues with those obtained from randomly generated data indicated a three-factor solution. Consequently, three factors were extracted for further analysis.

The three factors explained 14%, 13% and 10% of the variance, respectively. Together, the three factors accounted for 38% of the total variance. The χ 2 test of the hypothesis that three factors are sufficient was not significant, χ²(33) = 47.23, p = .052, indicating that the threefactor solution provides a good representation of the data. Goodness of fit indices were also indicative of good fit (SRMR = .04, RMSEA = .047, 90% CI [0, .076]).

Factor loadings are presented in Table 2. Inspection of factor loadings revealed a taskspecific rather than a domain-general structure. The first factor was mainly defined by the Segmentation task measures, including RT learning index and the 2AFC and production tests.

Interestingly, the accuracy learning index showed only a weak loading to this factor. The second factor was primarily defined by the TVSL task. The third factor was dominated by the ASRT RT learning index, with a modest contribution from the ASRT accuracy learning index.

Several measures, such as the SRT learning index, CC learning index, SVSL task and WPT, showed weak loadings and low communalities, indicating that they were not strongly associated with any of the extracted factors. Correlations among the factors were low to moderate (rs = .03-.27).

Overall, the factor structure was characterized by clusters of measures originating from the same task rather than by a single factor shared across SL paradigms, providing little evidence for a domain-general SL factor. Furthermore, we ran three robustness checks. First, to minimize the potential influence of outliers, we conducted trial-based outlier filtering for the online measures, then ran a factor analysis on these variables. Second, we standardized the online measures to ensure that individual differences in baseline processing speed do not influence our results and conducted a factor analysis on standardized variables. Third, instead of using the learning indices averaged over the whole task for the online measures, we used performance only at the end of the task (the last blocks of the online measures) and ran a factor analysis on these variables. The idea behind this approach is to bring closer the online and offline measures: originally, online measures represent learning over the whole task, while offline measures are administered only at the end of the task. This way, both measures represent performance at the end of the task.

Considering all three factor analyses, we found identical factor structures to the one on the original data. The details of each robustness check and the exact statistics of the three exploratory factor analyses can be found in the Supplementary Information (Section 1.3.).

4. Discussion

The present study examined the organization of individual differences across a broad battery of established visual SL paradigms. The correlational and factor-analytic results provided little evidence for a common latent individual-difference dimension in behavioral performance spanning the different visual SL paradigms. Instead, cross-task correlations were sparse and generally weak, whereas the three extracted factors were primarily defined by multiple measures originating from the same paradigm. More specifically, the first factor was characterized by the Segmentation measures, the second by the TVSL measures, whereas the third was primarily associated with the ASRT RT measure. This pattern remained stable across three complementary robustness analyses, suggesting that the observed organization of individual differences is unlikely to reflect a particular analytic decision. Importantly, however, participants showed robust evidence of learning at the group level in almost all paradigms, and the learning measures demonstrated generally adequate to good reliability. Thus, the limited convergence across tasks cannot be readily attributed to a general failure of the battery to elicit learning or to unreliable measurement. Taken together, these findings indicate that behavioral variance was organized more strongly within paradigms than across paradigms. The remainder of the Discussion considers what this organization implies for the structure and construct validity of behavioral measures of visual SL.

The extracted factors did not align with the major dimensions commonly used to classify SL tasks (e.g., Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017). Measures did not cluster according to motor involvement, online versus offline assessment, or shared statistical structures and stimulus domains (cf. Table 1). Had any one of these dimensions organized individual differences, tasks sharing that characteristic would have been expected to load together. The correlational analyses nevertheless indicated selective convergence across tasks.

Bayesian analyses provided strong to extreme evidence for several cross-task associations among offline measures, including between Segmentation and TVSL measures as well as between SVSL and TVSL production. Moderate evidence for convergence was also observed between the online RT measures of the Segmentation and ASRT tasks. Interestingly, strong to moderate evidence was found for a modest association between WPT and selected Segmentation and TVSL measures (see Figures 4 and S7). Thus, some cross-task commonality was clearly present, but it was selective rather than organized consistently along any of the task dimensions considered here.

At the level of the extracted factor structure, the strongest shared variance was instead observed among measures derived from the same SL paradigm. This pattern suggests that the broader task architecture, rather than any single task dimension considered here, constituted the most coherent unit of covariance in the present task battery. One way to conceptualize this is to view an observed behavioral SL score as reflecting both learning-related variance and measurement-specific variance arising from the broader task architecture. The latter includes systematic variance associated with the stimuli, exposure conditions, response requirements, assessment format, and other features through which SL is operationalized, as well as the cognitive processes recruited by these features. Hereafter, we use the term task-specific variance to refer to the non-random component of measurement-specific variance arising from the particular task architecture.

The Segmentation task provides the clearest illustration of the role of task architecture.

Three markedly different behavioral measuresan online RT index, an offline 2AFC recognition measure, and an offline production measureloaded on the same factor. These measures differ substantially in their immediate task requirements and in how acquired knowledge is expressed behaviorally; yet, despite these differences, they converged (cf. Siegelman, Bogaerts, Kronenfeld, et al., 2018). One important commonality is that they were derived from the same learning experience and indexed the same underlying statistical structure (but for the lack of within-task correlations between online and offline measures, see Vernaillen & Bogaerts (2026)). A similar pattern was observed for the TVSL and ASRT tasks, where different behavioral indices likewise clustered together despite differing in their response requirements or measurement types. Thus, distinctions that are often emphasized in the SL literatureincluding online versus offline assessment, processing-based versus reflectionbased measures (Batterink & Paller, 2017 , 2019; Bogaerts et al., 2025; Lukács et al., 2021; Schneider et al., 2022; Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017; Siegelman, Bogaerts, Kronenfeld, et al., 2018; Vernaillen & Bogaerts, 2026), and RT versus accuracy indices (Curran, 1997; Hikosaka et al., 1999 Hikosaka et al., , 2002;; Song et al., 2007; Takács et al., 2018) were not sufficient to explain the observed covariance structure. Instead, when the broader task architecture was held constant, different behavioral expressions of acquired knowledge captured shared individual-difference variance.

The present findings help clarify the apparently mixed results of previous multi-task studies of SL. Similar to Siegelman & Frost (2015), we found limited convergence across heterogeneous SL paradigms. This is notable because shared task variance in previous work has typically been reported for paradigms within the same modality or targeting the same type of regularity (Bogaerts et al., 2025). The present battery held modality constant across seven canonical paradigms and nevertheless yielded little convergence, indicating that withinmodality similarity is not in itself sufficient to produce shared individual-difference variance.

Likewise, Godfroid & Kim (2021) identified multiple latent dimensions across different learning paradigms (cf. Buffington et al., 2021). However, whereas their study primarily used learning paradigms to predict external cognitive abilities, the present study was specifically designed to examine the organization of SL measures themselves, providing a more direct test of convergence. Finally, although Kalra et al. (2019) reported some shared variance across SL tasks, their final one-factor solution excluded the artificial grammar learning task. Thus, their findings also point to substantial task specificity, rather than supporting a straightforward general SL factor. Overall, these studies are more consistent with the present findings than they may initially appear, although differences in task selection and study objectives complicate direct comparisons.

The findings of Growns et al. (2020) provide an important point of comparison. They found a prominent common component across four visual SL tasks. However, whereas Growns et al. (2020) systematically varied a limited set of task dimensions within a common experimental framework, the present study deliberately sampled paradigms that differ across multiple aspects of their task architecture. Consequently, the two studies tested generalization at different levels: across closely related task variants in Growns et al. (2020), and across heterogeneous canonical paradigms in the present study. Viewed together, these findings suggest that shared variance may be easier to detect when tasks are built within a common experimental framework and differ only along a limited number of theoretically relevant dimensions. In Growns et al. ( 2020), the tasks shared many features of their overall design, whereas the paradigms in the present study differed simultaneously in stimulus structure, temporal organization, response requirements, and how learning was measured. Such broader differences in task architecture may reduce the amount of shared variance observed across paradigms. Taken together, these findings raise the possibility that the organization of SL is hierarchical rather than unitary, with the extent of shared individual-difference variance depending on the degree of similarity among tasks. This interpretation has important implications for the construct validity of behavioral measures of SL.

Construct validity is one of the most pressing challenges in individual-differences research on SL (Bogaerts et al., 2025; Conway et al., 2025). Canonical paradigms are typically regarded as measures of SL because participants become sensitive to the embedded regularities at the group level. However, demonstrating a robust learning effect does not necessarily establish that between-person differences in the learning indices reflect variation in a common underlying SL ability. The present findings highlight the importance of distinguishing three complementary forms of evidence. First, a task must be sensitive to the experimental manipulation by reliably eliciting learning at the group level. Second, it should provide reliable estimates of individual differences. The present battery generally met both of these criteria.

Third, if behavioral performance across different paradigms is assumed to index the same individual-difference construct, the corresponding behavioral measures should demonstrate convergent validity by sharing systematic variance. Here, however, evidence for such convergence across paradigms was limited. Accordingly, the present findings suggest that robust learning effects and adequate reliability, although essential prerequisites for individualdifferences research, are not sufficient to establish that different behavioral indices capture the same underlying construct (Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017).

The measurement challenge described here is not unique to SL. A closely related problem emerged in the implicit-memory literature, where paradigms as varied as priming, skill learning, and conditioning were grouped under a single label despite differing substantially from one another at both the neural and the information-processing level. Willingham & Preuss (1995) took this concern to its logical conclusion in a paper titled The Death of Implicit Memory, arguing that the implicit phenomena were too heterogeneous among themselves to constitute a coherent superordinate construct, however clearly they could be dissociated from explicit memory. Comparable problems have been documented in other cognitive domains. Executive function tasks show weak cross-task correlations because each task recruits substantial non-executive processes, and although latent-variable modelling can partly recover structure from such data (Friedman & Robbins, 2022; Miyake et al., 2000), it does not always succeed: in a study closely comparable to ours in design and sample size, six established inhibitory control tasks yielded low zero-order correlations and no satisfactory latent model when reaction-time difference scores were used (Gärtner & Strobel, 2021).

Widely used measures of working memory have likewise been argued to lack convergent validity (Burgoyne et al., 2025). Visual SL therefore joins a broader class of constructs whose group-level robustness has not translated into convergent measurement at the level of individuals. This raises the question of how much of the observed divergence reflects the construct itself and how much reflects the way it is operationalized.

SL measures are not process-pure: in addition to sensitivity to the embedded regularities, performance depends on processes such as attention, executive functions, perceptual processing, memory, response selection, and decision making, whose relative contribution varies across paradigms (Nemeth & Tóth-Fáber, 2026; Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017). For example, performance in the ASRT task additionally depends on rapid visuomotor processing and response selection, whereas offline visual recognition measures place greater demands on perceptual discrimination, memory, and decision processes. Individual differences in these learning-independent processes can therefore obscure shared learning-related variance and weaken cross-paradigm correlations without necessarily implying the absence of a shared SL mechanism. The same issue complicates the interpretation of within-paradigm convergence. Measures derived from the same paradigm share not only the statistical regularities to be learned, but also stimuli, exposure conditions, perceptual demands, and other aspects of the task architecture (Bogaerts et al., 2021 (Bogaerts et al., , 2022;; Siegelman, Bogaerts, Christiansen, et al., 2017). Their covariance may therefore reflect both sensitivity to the embedded regularities and task-specific sources of variance. Consequently, the extracted factors should not be interpreted as reflecting only learning-related variance.

At the same time, the present results constrain a purely task-impurity account. Different measures derived from the same paradigm, particularly in the Segmentation task, shared substantial variance despite differing in their response and assessment requirements, whereas paradigms with several similar task characteristics, such as the ASRT and SRT, showed little correspondence (but see Buffington et al., 2021). If broad learning-independent task demands were the primary source of individual-difference variance, measures sharing those demands would be expected to show stronger convergence across paradigms. Yet, the strongest covariance was observed within paradigms even when the corresponding measures differed substantially in their immediate cognitive and response requirements. This does not imply that executive, attentional, or other task-specific processes make no contribution to performance; rather, variation in these processes appears insufficient to account for the dominant organization of covariance observed here. Importantly, however, the present analyses cannot determine whether the remaining within-paradigm covariance reflects statistical knowledge acquired within a particular task, sensitivity to particular forms of regularity, shared computational operations, or other aspects of the broader task architecture.

One possibility is that individual differences generalize selectively across particular statistical structures rather than across SL tasks as a whole. Paradigms differ not only in their spatial and temporal organization, but also in transition structure, probability distribution, and uncertainty. Distributional properties can influence learning at the group level; for example, Zipfian distributions have been shown to facilitate SL (Lavi-Rotbain & Arnon, 2021). It is therefore conceivable that individuals also differ in their sensitivity to particular probability structures or levels of uncertainty. More broadly, given the heterogeneity of statistical regularities encountered in natural environments, variability in sensitivity to different structures may not necessarily reflect limitations of a general learning mechanism, but could be compatible with a learning system adapted to acquiring diverse forms of environmental structure. This possibility remains speculative and was beyond the scope of the present study.

Therefore, the present results speak more directly to the organization of the behavioral measures currently used to operationalize SL than to the latent architecture of SL mechanisms themselves.

The interpretation of the factor structure should nevertheless be qualified by an important feature of the present study design. The Segmentation, TVSL, and ASRT tasks were each represented by multiple behavioral measures, whereas the SRT, contextual cueing, SVSL, and WPT tasks each contributed a single learning index. Consequently, the former could form task-specific covariance clusters, whereas the latter could not define latent dimensions on their own. To address this potential imbalance, we conducted an additional EFA in which each task was represented by a single variable (for details, see Section 1.3.4. in the Supplementary Information). In this analysis, no extractable factors were identified, suggesting that the absence of a general SL factor in the original analysis is unlikely to be attributable to inflated within-task shared variance resulting from including multiple variables from the same task.

Moreover, the emergence of three factors should not be interpreted as evidence that only the multiply measured paradigms reflect meaningful sources of individual variation. Rather, the more robust conclusion is that the single-indicator paradigms shared relatively little variance with the other behavioral measures included in the battery. Importantly, these paradigms were themselves theoretically diverse, encompassing deterministic sequential motor learning (SRT), spatial context-target learning during visual search (contextual cueing), spatial SL assessed by offline recognition (SVSL), and probabilistic cue-outcome learning with feedback (WPT).

Their weak associations are therefore unlikely to reflect a common characteristic separating them from the multiply measured paradigms. Instead, they further reinforce the conclusion that the present data do not support a simple higher-order classification of established visual SL tasks. Therefore, the strongest substantive finding of the present study is limited cross-task convergence, rather than the exact number or identity of the extracted factors.

Several features of the present study define both its strengths and the scope of its conclusions. Most importantly, the battery was designed to sample widely used visual SL tasks together with the behavioral learning indices by which they are most commonly operationalized in the literature. Consequently, the tasks were represented by different numbers of behavioral measures. This asymmetry in the number of measures per task also reflects the current state of the field rather than an arbitrary feature of the present design. The aim was not to construct a psychometrically balanced measurement battery, but to examine how currently used behavioral measures are organized at the level of individual differences. A second important design consideration is that the battery was intentionally restricted to the visual modality (cf. Growns et al., 2020). This limits the extent to which the present findings can be generalized across sensory modalities. However, holding modality constant was also a major strength of the study, as the present findings suggest that substantial task specificity remains even after this major source of heterogeneity is removed (cf. Frost et al., 2015; Siegelman & Frost, 2015).

Future research should build on these findings by bridging the gap between broad batteries of canonical SL paradigms and experimentally controlled task families (e.g., Growns et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2024). Broad batteries capture the diversity of behavioral measures used to operationalize SL, whereas controlled task families allow relevant task dimensions to be manipulated while holding the broader task architecture constant. Combining these complementary approaches would provide a promising direction. For example, researchers could develop task batteries in which multiple paradigms systematically sample the same task dimension (e.g., statistical structure or dependency type), while each paradigm is represented by multiple behavioral measures. Such designs would make it possible to determine whether shared variance reflects the intended task dimension or the broader task architecture in which it is embedded. They would also reduce the interpretational asymmetry between paradigms represented by single versus multiple indicators.

Finally, future work may benefit from moving beyond treating canonical paradigms as unitary measures of SL toward decomposing them into their constituent cognitive processes and computational operations (cf. Bogaerts et al., 2022; Nemeth & Tóth-Fáber, 2026). Processlevel behavioral measures and computational modeling may help disentangle the multiple operations involved in acquiring and expressing statistical knowledge (e.g., Éltető et al., 2022; Székely et al., 2024; Thiessen et al., 2013; Török et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023). Such approaches may also help determine which aspects of the covariance observed within paradigms arise from shared computational operations and which reflect other features of the broader task architecture. This could provide a stronger basis for identifying which components of individual differences genuinely reflect sensitivity to statistical regularities. Ultimately, progress in understanding individual differences in SL will require moving beyond asking whether tasks correlate toward identifying the specific sources of behavioral variance that generalize across paradigms and those that remain paradigm specific.

Conclusions

The present study mapped the covariance structure of a broad battery of canonical visual SL paradigms and their behavioral measures. Despite robust group-level learning and generally adequate reliability, these measures showed limited convergence across paradigms. Instead, behavioral variance was organized primarily within paradigms, with the strongest shared variance observed among different measures derived from the same task. This organization was not readily explained by commonly proposed task dimensions, such as online versus offline assessment, motor involvement, or the underlying statistical structure. Together, these findings provide limited support for treating performance across established visual SL paradigms as manifestations of a single latent individual-difference construct. Importantly, this limited behavioral convergence does not determine whether the paradigms rely on shared or distinct SL mechanisms, because the observed measures may also incorporate task-specific perceptual, cognitive, and response-related processes. Instead, the present findings highlight the need to better distinguish learning-related variance from task-specific sources of behavioral variance. This will require combining the breadth of canonical task batteries with the experimental control of systematically designed task families to identify which cognitive and computational processes can be generalized. A clearer understanding of generalizability may eventually improve the interpretation of individual differences in domains where SL has been implicated, including language and reading development.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Schematic illustration of the tasks. (A) In the ASRT task, a target stimulus in one of the four horizontal cues was presented. Participants were instructed to press the corresponding button as fast and as accurately as possible. (B)In the SRT task, participants were presented with a target stimulus (a white rectangle) in one of the four possible horizontally arranged positions (blank rectangles) on the screen. Similarly to the ASRT task, the instruction was to press the corresponding button as fast and as accurately as possible. (C) In the Segmentation task, participants were presented with a continuous stream of non-figurative symbols while performing a target detection task. The target stimulus is marked with a red outline for illustration purposes, but it was not marked to the participants during the task. (D) In the TVSL task, a continuous stream of non-figurative symbols was presented sequentially at the center of the screen. During the stimulus presentation, participants were instructed to pay attention but they did not need to press any buttons. (E) In the SVSL task, complex visual scenes of abstract shapes arranged within a spatial grid were presented to the participants. They were instructed to pay attention but were not required to make any responses. (F) In the CC task, participants searched for a rotated letter T embedded among rotated L distractors and responded as quickly and accurately as possible to the target's orientation. (G) In the weather prediction task (WPT), participants predicted whether the outcome would be "sun" or "rain" based on combinations of one to three cue cards displaying geometric patterns. Each cue card was probabilistically associated with one of the two outcomes.
